newsitem.title: USA: NHL-FETISOV RELEASED, KONSTANTINOV IN COMA BUT SEEN RECOVERING.
newsitem.headline: NHL-FETISOV RELEASED, KONSTANTINOV IN COMA BUT SEEN RECOVERING.

text.p: Detroit Red Wings defenceman Slava Fetisov, showing no lingering effects from a limousine crash five days ago, left the hospital Wednesday but pleaded with fans to pray for his critically injured Russian teammate and a team trainer.

Doctors at Beaumont Hospital in suburban Birmingham issued a hopeful prognosis for star defenceman Vladimir Konstantinov and trainer Sergei Mnatsakanov, who both suffered severe head injuries in the June 13 accident and have only slowly begun emerging from comas.
"While I'm happy to be going home, Vladi and Sergei still need your thoughts and prayers," the Russian-born Fetisov, 39, said.
Fellow Russians Konstantinov, 30, and Mnatsakanov, 43, were both responding to voices, and Konstantinov had opened his eyes but without focusing, neurosurgeon Karol Zakalik told reporters.

"We can't guarantee that he will have a full recovery but it certainly makes me optimistic," said Zakalik, who added that Konstantinov has opened his eyes and wiggled his toes, responding to friends' commands spoken in Russian.

Konstantinov, nicknamed "The Vladinator" for his punishing physical style, is one of three finalists for the Norris Trophy as the National Hockey League's top defencemen. The NHL will give out its awards on Thursday night.
Fetisov, seated behind the driver, suffered chest contusions and a bruised lung when the stretch limousine they were riding in careened off the road and struck a tree head-on.
"I wanted to thank the fans for all the cards and gifts, especially from the kids," said Fetisov, who was among the first wave of Russian players to break into the NHL.
Investigators suspect that limousine driver Richard Gnida, who was driving with a suspended license, fell asleep at the wheel. Gnida, 28, was released from hospital on Sunday.

Konstantinov and Fetisov are two of the team's vaunted "Russian Five" players who were instrumental in helping capture the team's first Stanley Cup in 42 years, breaking the longest championship drought among National Hockey League teams.
